issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court may not set aside factual findings of a subordinate tribunal merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The appellate rent court granted eviction on the basis of factual findings drawn from the evidence before it.
The reviewing court relied on material that had not been before the rent court and disturbed its findings.
The Supreme Court found no basis to treat the rent court’s findings as perverse or so unreasonable that no court could have reached them.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by disturbing the eviction decree on those grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers judicial superintendence, not appellate jurisdiction to re-examine evidence or correct mere factual errors. Intervention is confined to keeping subordinate courts within their authority and is justified where findings are perverse or so unreasonable that no court could have reached them. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte, M/s. India Pipe Fitting Co. v. Fakruddin M.A. Baker, and Sukhbir Narain v. Deputy Director of Consolidation.

rule.if: supervisory_review and findings_based_on_evidence and not findings_perverse_or_unreasonable

predicates.supervisory_review: A court reviews a subordinate court or tribunal in the exercise of supervisory rather than appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.findings_based_on_evidence: The subordinate court or tribunal reached its factual findings on the evidence before it.
predicates.findings_perverse_or_unreasonable: The subordinate court or tribunal’s factual findings are so perverse or unreasonable that no court could have reached them.
predicates.supervisory_court_must_not_disturb_factu: The supervisory court does not disturb the subordinate court or tribunal’s factual findings.

issues.definition: When a supervisory court reviews factual findings reached on evidence, it must leave them undisturbed unless they are perverse or so unreasonable that no court could have reached them.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may obtain eviction for personal occupation when the need is reasonable and bona fide and refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting it would cause the tenant.
material_facts: The landlady lived with several family members in a small apartment with one bedroom, while another son lived separately with his own family.
The tenant occupied a flat in the same locality that he admitted had a kitchen and three rooms.
The landlady sought additional accommodation for her family, and the tenant produced no evidence that her demand was made for an oblique motive.
The circumstances showed that refusing eviction would leave the landlady’s family facing greater hardship than the tenant would face upon eviction.
issues.conclusion: The landlady’s need was reasonable and bona fide, and the comparative hardship did not bar eviction; the eviction decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 requires a reasonable and bona fide need for the landlord’s occupation. Under Section 13(2), eviction is barred if the tenant would suffer greater hardship from eviction than the landlord would suffer from refusal. Reasonableness depends on the circumstances of the case; the Court relied on Krishchand Moorjimal v. Bai Kalavati, Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Jagan Nath Ashok Kumar, and Gujarat Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. Unique Erectors (Gujarat) Pvt. Ltd. The circumstances supported a presumption of bona fides, which remained unrebutted in the absence of evidence of an oblique motive.

predicates.personal_occupation_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks eviction so that the landlord can occupy the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_has_inadequate_accommodation_fo: The landlord’s existing accommodation is inadequate for the size or needs of the household.
predicates.tenant_has_not_shown_oblique_motive: The tenant has produced no evidence that the landlord’s demand is made for an improper or oblique purpose.
predicates.landlord_would_suffer_greater_hardship_t: Refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting eviction would cause the tenant.
predicates.eviction_for_landlords_occupation_is_jus: The landlord is entitled to eviction for the landlord’s occupation.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeking personal occupation lacks adequate accommodation, the tenant shows no oblique motive, and refusal would cause the landlord greater hardship, eviction for the landlord’s occupation is justified.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction for personal occupation is not required to specify the floor area of the landlord’s existing accommodation.
material_facts: The reviewing court faulted the landlady for not specifying the floor area of her existing accommodation.
Her affidavit in the reviewing court in fact stated the area and described the rooms in the apartment.
The Supreme Court held that the governing eviction ground imposed no legal requirement to specify the area in the landlord’s possession.
issues.conclusion: Failure to specify the floor area of existing accommodation is not a legal bar to an eviction claim based on the landlord’s need for occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 requires reasonable and bona fide need for occupation, but does not require the landlord to specify the floor area of the accommodation already occupied.

predicates.personal_occupation_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks eviction so that the landlord can occupy the rented premises.
predicates.failure_to_specify_existing_floor_area_i: The absence of a stated floor area for the landlord’s existing accommodation does not, by itself, defeat the eviction claim.

issues.definition: In a claim for eviction for a landlord’s personal occupation, not stating the floor area of existing accommodation does not by itself defeat the claim.
